utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Ierace, is the Prosecution ready to present its rebuttal evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We will do that. Two preliminary matters: Because the evidence refers to a protected witness and involves a photograph, it would seem that closed session would be the appropriate format in which that evidence is to be taken. And secondly, rather than tender the 92 bis statement, it might be easier all round if I take a few minutes to orally elicit the evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As you may remember last Friday, the Chamber has explicitly left it up to the Prosecution whether they wanted to present the 92 bis statement. And then, of course, parts should have been taken out, because only to some extent the rebuttal evidence was allowed. And since the 92 bis statement also deals with other matters, perhaps that might be the most practical way of presenting this evidence. But before giving a decision, is there any observation to be made from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, good morning. None at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then about closed session, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is there any ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I believe that with good reason Mr. Galic, General Galic, tells me that the fact that it's a protected witness does not necessarily require a closed session. We could perhaps deal with the once and this photograph in closed session in certain parts, as far as the photograph is concerned, but not entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Apart from that. But Mr. Ierace, would you agree to go into closed session whenever any issue arises in respect of the protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Or alternatively, I could place some yellow stickers over the identifying features of the witness's body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then, of course, the witness should be instructed to -- not to mention the name of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: He has those instructions already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He has those instructions. Okay. Then we might even avoid at all to go into closed session. Then, Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. I take it that you're Mr. Tait-Harris?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. Good morning, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't have to ask you whether you understand me in a language -- whether you hear me in a language you understand, since you replied to my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tait-Harris, before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text will be handed out to you now by the usher and I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Tait-Harris, as far as I understand, your testimony will be about your investigative activities, also in relation to a person who is a protected -- who was a protected witness in this case. May I -- although I do understand that you might have received already instructions, would you please not mention the name of any protected witness in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if there would be a necessity to do so, we'll turn into closed session first. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is your full name Jonathan Hopwood Tait-Harris?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born on the 1st of February, 1962?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you an investigator with the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how many years have you held that position?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Four and a half years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that, what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: I was a detective officer with the West Mercia constabulary in Great Britain.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask the witness be shown P3808. I have copies, one for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this is going very fast, I didn't hear very well where he was a detective, because it's not on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Please could you repeat in what police force, as I understand, you were serving before you came to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The West Mercia constabulary, which is a police service based in the midwest of Great Britain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I do not know what yellow stickers you used exactly, but there is no other -- is there any name on it, or is that the name of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That would be the name of this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you please place the photograph in front of you complete with the yellow sticker on the machine to your right.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what date did you take the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: The 5th of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by reference to pseudonyms, who is it that appears in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: This is a gentleman known as Witness G.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One additional question: The 5th of March would be of this year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good morning. What are your titles, degrees, academic titles?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President, on the grounds of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, gladly. I note that this is the first and, I hope, the last objection. If the witness leaves the courtroom, I'll explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Well, the objection is about relevance. I do understand that Mr. Ierace points at the fact that this witness has been called exclusively to establish the source of this photograph, and I do understand that Mr. Ierace takes the position that whether you take a photograph with or without any academic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well. Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. We'll ask Mr. Tait-Harris to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it's all right. I'm -- I'm going to ask another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the sensitivity that you used?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: May I ask in what respect?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the photograph. What is the sensitivity of this? When we're talking about photography, there are films of various sensitivity. ASA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you asking about what is usually called the DIN or the ASA value of the film that has been used?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: I understand the question now. The film -- sorry, the image was recorded with a digital camera, so therefore film was not an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how did you print this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: This photograph was printed directly from the compact disk onto which the images were downloaded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do it yourself, the printing?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: I requested it to be printed, but no, I didn't print it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you gave that CD to someone else.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: No, no. The image was printed directly off our internal computer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did the printing?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Our photo visuals unit. If I may explain the procedure, it's quite straightforward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, not for the moment. I would only like to know: What is the machine you used to take this photograph, the camera?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: A digital camera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But which one, which type?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Excuse me if I don't know, but it's one that was issued to me by our equipment department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know whether with this type of camera you can rewind the image?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It must be an interpreting matter. Can you turn the image back?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Can I make comment on the question before. I didn't actually hear that question. So the answer I see before me is not what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think the question is whether you can -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sinus cosinus. Sinus cosinus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether you can mirror the image, so left to the right, right to the left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On that camera.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Generally speaking, in all the mechanisms known to us, computer mechanisms, and we know it, it is possible to reverse the image on a photograph. Do you know -- no, I'm going to rephrase this question. And kindly focus on the question that follows. I am talking about the print that we have in front of us. How can I know - and I'm talking only about the print now - how can I know without the negative, the original negative, whether this photo is a reflection of what the camera saw or if it is reversed? I'm not talking about the situation. I'm talking only about this image, this print. Have you understood the question?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Yes, I have entirely. The photograph we have before us is the photograph that I took, and I believe it hasn't been reversed because of the fact I can relate it to other items in the room. But with regards to whether it's possible with this camera, I cannot comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this camera allow you to make close-ups?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: It does in the respect it has a limited zoom capability.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What distance?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: I don't know what the focal length of the lens is. It's the case that when you look through it, you can zoom in and out until it frames the photograph to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you went on that mission, did you know what that mission was? Did you know what you were supposed to photograph?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: I was aware that I had to photograph this subject and this part of the subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which part?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: The gentleman's rear view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But his entire body, the rear view of his entire body, or a certain part of it?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: His upper rear body was the area in which I had particular interest, and I asked him to expose the area that had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what kind of wound it was allegedly?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: I was aware that they were -- the marks that I was particularly to focus on would be consistent with that of a bullet wound. But as for any more detail than that, no, I wasn't aware.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before leaving, did you try to make a test of your camera to see until what distance you could photograph with the zoom to have as many details as possible?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: If I understand your question correctly, you're asking me could I have got closer to make a more detailed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I asked you whether you made a preliminary test.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: No. Because the view finder gives you -- you see in the view finder the image you will receive once the photograph is taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That, I understand. But my question is whether - yes or no - you made a test. For instance, did a colleague of yours draw something on his back for you to test the camera and see how close you can get?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. With the assistance of the usher, I would like you to look at another photograph and use the Post-its so that we can have maximum protection of the subject. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Put a Post-it also on the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The signature -- it is the signature of this witness, as we just have established, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I want it to be protected, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This witness is not protected in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I'm sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness, would you kindly point the wound with a pointer, the entrance wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The question presumes that this witness from one source or another is aware of which is the entrance wound and which is the exit wound, and that hasn't been at all established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please first lay the foundation for this last question. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll rephrase that, Mr. President. But could the booth follow me closely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please point to the area where we can see a wound in this image.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, again the question assumes there is only one wound which is visible, and that hasn't been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is there the trace of a wound of any kind on this part of the person, on this side of the person; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please point to the wound that we can see or the wound that you think you can identify.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness complied and pointed once to the upper part and then to the bottom part to the left towards the interior, not towards the exterior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat that, because I do not see everything appearing in the transcript, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I asked that I should be closely followed. I'll repeat that. The witness started by pointing to the upper part of the right -- of the back on the right. That's not the case, but -- the right --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if the booth can't translate, they should say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I --.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there a problem? If so, I'll change my terminology. In the upper part, below the shoulder, to the right there's the first wound. And then the second wound, it's to the left near the spine, the shoulder blade to the left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you pointed to the right, below the right spatula [as interpreted] on the back of the patient --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't the spatula, but it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You pointed to there. Is it possible - yes or no - to make a close-up of this?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Not without removing the witness's visual features, which I included so that we could link the photograph of the upper torso to the person's identity, i.e., the head. To go in any closer would have been just the relate or would have just resulted in purely a picture of the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know whether there are medical reports which have to do -- which concern this witness; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. I note that it's 15 minutes, firstly. Secondly, this goes well beyond the scope of rebuttal and therefore the scope of cross-examination, in my respectful submission, a very different rule applies to cross-examination of a rebuttal witness in terms of latitude. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't agree. But it's not the first time that I don't agree with my colleague, Mr. Ierace. And it's for the reason -- for the following reason: We know that if we want to have a clear idea of this, we have to have the trace of the wound somewhere. It has to be visible. Our medical expert on the basis of such photographs would have liked to tell us something, to inform us of something, but we have great difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Whether this -- whether this witness knows anything about medical reports in respect of the person he photographed. Do you know anything about medical reports in respect of this -- of this part of the body of Witness G?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm going to be very cautious in my answer here. About this photograph, Mr. President, no. But I'm aware that certain medical records do exist for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you consult them before taking this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did read them, but my aim in taking this photograph was to record an image, and it wasn't, I believe, necessary to go into any greater detail than establish this person had wounds upon his back so that I knew what area to photograph and that I could discuss that with him so that I got the right photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a former detective in the police force, did you ever have the opportunity in the course of your professional life of using cameras; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: In my years with the West Mercia constabulary, no, that was not the role of a detective. We had other persons to work with to do that task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other situations perhaps, here in the OTP?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Yes. I have used cameras and video cameras before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that you've used cameras, would that include classical cameras with film?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Various types of camera, including film camera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, do you know whether in the course of investigations, police investigations, it is sometimes useful to see details, that is to say, to have close-ups --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I know Judges who immediately seize mobile phones that are --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I have a problem with my -- with my device because I can't see when it's on, when it's all. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm sure that my colleague is trying to remind me that time is running out, and I'll take that into account.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, this will be my last question: Do you know whether in the course of police investigations it is sometimes necessary to have a detail available, that is to say, to have a close-up of certain elements which are of particular importance for an investigation? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Witness, would you have had the possibility, the technical possibility in the OTP, within the OTP to take a traditional device with you for investigation of yours which might have enabled us to have a close-up and to have the appropriate lens to have a close-up of these two alleged points of impact? Did you have such a possibility; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: The equipment was available. It would not have made the photograph attributable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For what reason?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Quite simply the case that the photograph was taken as such so that we could attribute it to this particular witness. The equipment required would be quite simple and the equipment that we took this with, that this was taken --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'll stop you there. Why did you provide me with this answer? I simply asked you whether the material existed -- the equipment existed. You made a comment. Why did you add this comment?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: So that my answer was understood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was simple: Was there such equipment; yes or no? Would it have been possible - yes or no - to make a close-up of these two points or -- that is, of the upper part of the back; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Is there any need to re-examine the witness, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just one matter, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Re-examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have in front of you a black pen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want markings to be made, Mr. Ierace, blue was the colour --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. Blue, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please take the blue pen and circle the two wounds that you indicated earlier, being very careful as you do so to not actually obscure the wounds themselves. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps just one question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Further cross-examination by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you take the pointer. Can you see the first part of the right -- the anterior, the forward part of the right elbow?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand. I can see his right elbow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Of course you can see it. The anterior part of the right elbow, the fore part. [In English] The right part of his elbow, please, can you see it?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: If you're referring to this area here, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's exactly that. Do you see anything here, a hole maybe?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: I can see wrinkles and a dark area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point to that spot, please.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you see a hole here? Can you see a hole?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: I can see a mark, but I don't know whether it's a hole or not. I can't comment on whether it's a hole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. No comment at all. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Did you take one photograph only or more than one photograph?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Four photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Do you have them?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Not with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have some black-and-white copies of those if you wish to see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes. But I think that we should see them on the ELMO, the colour photographs as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I'll hand those up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we also take care that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- The face of the person photographed is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. And I don't have colour photocopies, only black and white.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They could be produced if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: They could, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll have to intervene with regard to a problem of disclosure concerning this witness. And could the Prosecution provide us with these elements as soon as possible because we are quite surprised to discover about their existence now. I didn't ask the witness because I was sure there was one photograph. That changes everything. We'll have to prepare for this witness for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- if I could respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I don't accept that the disclosure obligations require -- will require the Prosecution in this case to disclose to the Defence every photograph taken by this witness of Witness G. I see no basis for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't think that's the case. We're trying to find the truth here and not play a game of hide and seek. The Prosecution has had these photographs since March, I think, so for long enough, and I don't see why we weren't informed of this immediately. We've had to try and contact our expert, ask the expert questions, and we're not ready today, so we are saying that there's been a violation of our rights. This seems to me to be a manoeuvre which violates the Rules, and it's not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What Rule exactly, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that when we have -- when one has material -- I haven't seen these photographs yet. If there is material --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What Rule exactly, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, I think that with regard to respect for fair proceedings, the accused should know exactly what is being done. And when one continues with an investigation, all the elements of the investigation should be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was asking you what Rule exactly, perhaps apart from --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Rule 66 should provide an answer to that question. But unfortunately I don't know this by heart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Rule 66(B) says that "The Prosecutor shall on request permit the Defence to inspect any books, documents, photographs, and tangible objects in the Prosecutor's custody or control which are material to the preparation of the Defence or are intended for use by the Prosecutor as evidence at trial or were obtained from or belonged to the accused." Isn't it -- that would be Rule 66(B), which starts with a request. And I'm just trying to -- because I'm trying to find, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Rule which says that the material, also those parts that are not used in evidence, should have been disclosed to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But, Mr. President, I think that there is a general principle, especially if we have such a delicate question and something that has to be dealt with by experts, because we have seen that the experts don't share the same opinion. When we continue with investigations and additional elements are provided, I don't think that one can content oneself with simply providing the best of. Everything that's been photographed should be provided or nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I have no further questions. I have the photographs. That's all. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know that the Defence is sometimes perfectionist, and we would be glad -- we'd appreciate it if we could have these photos in colour, if there are any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I understand, they have to be printed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be correct, yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's possible and that doesn't take too much time, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't believe it will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question for you: Did you look closely to the part of the body of Witness G you were to photograph?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Yes. But -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see anything on this part of his body, apart from the two spots you just indicated which to you, as not a medical expert, looked as if this was a scar of a previous wound?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Mr. Tait-Harris, since you've answered all the questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not quite, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that you would like to put another question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've just said this, and I'll say it even more clearly: We worked in the dark to a certain extent because our expert wasn't able to - and I'll show this -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... That's not the testimony of this witness. What I do understand is that you want to have oral arguments on disclosure issues which eventually might lead you to further requests or submissions to the Chamber, and perhaps that therefore you would like to remain this witness available or his photographs available. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Mr. President. But what I wanted to say before we release the witness, the Defence reserves its rights. Because when we asked for the assistance of an expert to get prepared, he was incapable for seeing -- of seeing a possible wound on the back in the photographs that were given to us. So now perhaps we'll be able to work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace, we therefore can expect that the Defence might submit a request for further cross-examination of this witness in respect of other photographs shown. The status of these other photographs is not entirely clear to me at this moment because it's not clear to me what photographs you'll tender as exhibits. Is that only the coloured photograph or also the black-and-white photographs that have been shown to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm happy to tender the black-and-white photographs as well if that's of assistance to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just in order to clarify issues, may I ask you,

utterances.speaker: MR. TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: One of these four photographs seems to be part of the coloured photograph; is that right? And I am looking at the bottom of these pages. There's one which bears the number -- yes. Could that please be shown -- 1106.JPG and is not the entire --

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: This black-and-white photograph that I see here does appear to be slightly smaller than the -- than the image, but the file number which you see at the bottom left-hand corner is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I have to understand that all of these black-and-white photographs are parts of the original photographs? Because they all end at 5.3 and then do not give any further details in respect of the dates, and I can imagine that this has been caused by the landscape versus the portrait format of the --

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: The reproduction, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the reproduction.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: I believe that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ierace, if you want to -- if all these documents are -- all the photographs are tendered, would it not be wise to provide coloured photographs but then the full photograph and not only part of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I imagine we can obtain colour copies during the course of the day, if that's of any assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tait-Harris, this at least for this moment concludes your evidence before this Trial Chamber. As you may have noticed --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. It's just been brought to my attention that there may be a further photograph which is not included in the black-and-white copies. I'll provide a copy of that as well to my learned colleagues during the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that would raise the issue whether there was a fifth photograph and the number "5" seems to be a problematic one in this courtroom. Mr. Tait-Harris, was it your evidence that you took four photographs or ...?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Yes. I said four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a question now because the fifth photograph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, could you explain to this Chamber how you could produce a fifth photograph where the witness says that he has taken four?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I can explain that. Perhaps I should do that in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, may I ask you to escort Mr. Tait-Harris out of the courtroom for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. President, what prompts me to say is that is that I have an e-mail from Mr. Tait-Harris to myself dated the 13th of March, 2003 on which there is a further image. The email included electronically copies of the photographs we've so far seen and a further one. So I suspect that he's forgotten that one. I should hasten to add I don't think it changes the situation at all in terms of the quality of the evidence. But just to be complete on it, I think there is a fifth photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- we should ask the witness. Could you tell us -- he has sent these photographs electronically to you by email?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there were five. And they all cover the same subject? It's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you allow me a minute, Mr. President, just to double-check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, if you would look at the black-and-white copies you see that the file numbers are indicated, and Judge Nieto-Navia draws my attention to the fact that it goes from 1103 to 1105 and then 6 and 7, so one would expect that once there existed an 1104.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think actually the further photograph I have is the number 2 rather than the number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And does that also show the back of Witness G or --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we should ask the witness in more detail about that. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you for 02, but 04 is missing, so from 5 we'll probably be reaching number 6, so we should deal with this on one occasion, at once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If Mr. Ierace could inform us -- he only talked about five photographs and not of six, but if he has any knowledge of a sixth photograph which could be 1104, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's then ask the witness. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tait-Harris, there's still a few questions remaining. You testified that you took four photographs. We have been informed that you once sent an email with attached to it electronic photographs of the same subject but that there were five.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: I apologise if that is the case. I must be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please look on the black-and-white photographs, if they could be put in front of you again. We see -- on the black-and-white ones we see the file names. What the Chamber has in front of it is file numbers 1103.JPG, 1105, 1106, and 1107. You'll find that on the bottom of the page printed out. Are you aware of the existence of 1104 and perhaps 1102 and/or 1108? I mean, there's one missing in the series, and of course it's still to be established whether 1103 would be the first one of the series and whether 1107 would be the last one of the series.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not aware of the existence of other photographs that perhaps would slot into this sequence of numbers. When I take the photographs with this camera, I merely switch the camera on and begin to photograph them. The file number doesn't appear until the time when you come to download them, if that's a good way of explaining it. And as to how the camera numbers these photographs, these are numbered by the camera rather than myself. And if they're out of sequence, then that is possibly down to a technical explanation that I don't -- that I'm not able to offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the next question would be: Did you take any photograph at that time of which you thought it was, for example, for technical reasons not satisfactory and that, therefore, you removed it, which in -- with many cameras one can do?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: There was a further photograph, and it was sideways on, if I may use that term, in landscape as opposed to portrait. I haven't removed it. It still exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any further questions in respect of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible that there was -- that there is one, but I would like to consult my co-counsel, if you allow me first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No other questions, but just a suggestion to the Prosecution so that we can save time. Would it be possible for the Prosecution to give us a computer copy of the photographs they received. If that's possible, we could immediately do what is required, send it to one of our experts, to save time, and after that we could hear again this witness. It's just a matter of practical saving of time. We could have a computer copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I certainly have -- I'm certainly happy to provide electronic copies of the photographs. I wouldn't want that to be interpreted as an acceptance by the Prosecution of the need to recall the witness. Might I make a suggestion, and that is that we quickly print off this further photograph so that we can from the Prosecution perspective, at least, complete the evidence of this witness promptly, at least in black and white, if not colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. The Defence will not be helped much if they think we can prepare like that on the technical level. We need time to consult our experts. At this time we cannot immediately be ready and continue the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, if you could provide a electronic version of all photographs available to you to the Defence, that would be fair. I do understand that the Defence reserves its right to ask this witness to be recalled for further cross-examination. The Chamber will consider that matter. And if you are preparing an electronic version, and I do understand that it's not your intention to file it but the Chamber would like to have an electronic copy as well because it enables to enlarge and to do a lot of things in order to have a better look at these photographs. But apart from that, the Chamber would like to have all the photographs taken, whether there are five or six, in evidence in coloured copies. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honor. I think we have the same view of things. One of the reasons - and I thank you for this suggestion - what we wanted is to have photographs showing certain areas. And when you enlarge the photograph, you can see whether it is reversed or not. They always go in this -- in the same direction. Certain things are always juxtaposed in a certain way. So if you have a picture in the photograph, you will be able to see whether it was reversed or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you please be very careful in having pictures in your hand while standing because the booth cannot guarantee that not part of those pictures are not seen on the screen. I can imagine that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake. I'll take something else to hold it rather than a photograph. My mistake and apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Tait-Harris --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. I seek leave to ask a question or two following on the last answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That directly arises from the questions from the Bench, I take it. Please do so, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Further examination by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said there was a further photograph and it was sideways on, if I may use that term, in landscape as opposed to portrait. The photograph that you were first shown this morning was in what format, landscape or portrait?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: The one this morning was landscaped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The photograph that you described as still existing, that you haven't removed, as best as you recollect is that in landscape or portrait?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS
utterances.text: On the computer screen, the image of the witness lies sideways. But whether it's actually in a portrait or a landscape background, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Mr. Tait-Harris, I'll try it once again, to tell you that this concludes for the time being your evidence before this Trial Chamber. You may have noticed that there might be a moment where the parties or the Chamber would like to call you again as a witness. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if it assists, I now have some black-and-white copies of that photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, at least we could have a look at it not in order to take final decisions but at least to convince ourselves that it's about the same subject. Could they be distributed. Mr. Usher, could you please assist Mr. Ierace. In order to avoid any confusion, what we see in front of us now seems to be also a part -- a black-and-white copy of a part of a photograph which appears to have been taken as portrait rather than in landscape.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. As the witness was telling us, if this is something that was photographed sideways, it's not the impression I have when I look at this. So I don't know if we could ask the witness before releasing him if it's exactly the picture that he remembers or if he meant perhaps 04. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could perhaps the black-and-white copy be shown to the witness. It's already there. Mr. Tait-Harris, we're looking at the black-and-white photograph of which appears on the bottom "1102.JPG". Is this what you described as a photograph sideways taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That was not the evidence. If I could direct you to page 28, line 8, the witness referred to the image being sideways on the computer screen rather than the way it was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is this the picture you were talking about before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, before I -- I confirm that it is, I would like to actually check my image on a computer screen. I believe that this is the same photograph, but I would actually like to see the computer screen image. The reason I had difficulties, I tried to reproduce this by printing it and my image would not come out. That might be due to my lack of technical knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or sufficient technical knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For various reasons the Chamber deems this not necessary at this very moment for you to verify whether this was the picture you had in mind. If needed, if you would be recalled, then of course we could pay further attention to it. But at this moment that's not necessary. Mr. Ierace, the Chamber would also like to have a colour version of this complete photograph. Mr. Tait-Harris, I'm first looking to the parties before I give it a final try to see whether this really concludes for at this very moment your evidence -- your testimony in this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one remark: Because this witness is going to check this in his computer, let him also check --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the Chamber has decided that it was not necessary for him to check it at this moment. But if there would be anything else, because if he would be recalled, if there would be anything else you'd like him to check, please tell us now so that, Mr. Tait-Harris, that if you would receive a message that you would have to testify again, that apart from checking this photograph, that -- what else, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you would like him to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Simply, I would like us to be certain whether there were four or five or seven photographs, because the series does not go in sequence, some numbers are missing. So let the witness check if there were five, six, or seven, or more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you'll check on your computer as well whether we now have seen all the photographs or that there were any other photographs, but of course same subject, that means the back of Witness G. Well, this concludes for the time being your evidence in this court. Since there's a chance that you'll be recalled, I would like you not to discuss with anyone the subject of your testimony, also not in the near future. That does not mean that you're not allowed to work on it or that you would not be allowed to give instructions as such as to make printouts and give instructions on how to do that, but that you're not permitted to discuss the wounds, the situation of the wounds, what this could prove or not. So I'd like to instruct you not to discuss such issues with anyone unless -- up till the moment that it's for certain that you'd not have to appear again as a witness in relation to these photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Usher, would you please escort Mr. Tait-Harris out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the photographs -- the colour photographs could be made available to the Defence by today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The black-and-white photographs, as they have been shown to us, will be marked for identification so that we later can check whether the colour copies of the full photographs is the same as the black-and-white cutout. And then I take it that you already tender at this moment as P3808 the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Photograph which has been provided in colour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the photographs marked for identification will be MFI.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is a set of photographs on which appears on the bottom the file number --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. I made an error. It's MFI.32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is a bundle of black-and-white photographs which a file indication on the bottom of the page, last numbers 1102, 1103, 1105, 1106, and 1107 before the extension "JPG." Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also, this bundle of black-and-white photographs is marked for identification but under seal. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, Ms. Pilipovic, may I invite the Defence to express itself, apart from on the issue of these photographs, the additional photographs, what the Defence intends to present as evidence in rejoinder, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We believe that there should be one. We learned about the existence of new elements at the last minute, and these elements are certainly important. What we wanted and the Defence team will have to consult some more about the new photographs we will soon receive in colour, I hope -- we will have to express only a part of our views today. We wanted the expert who had to -- the opportunity of reviewing this sniping incident, Dr. Dunjic, to receive these photographs and equipped with the knowledge he has of the events in question - I regret to say that this particular expert is now engaged in working in the investigation of a very important assassination in Yugoslavia - so we wanted this expert to come to the court and based on all of these photographs to explain whether what he said during his first testimony still holds or not. I think it is important for him to come as a forensic expert and tell us his views. I believe we owe it to the defence of General Galic. Apart from that, we will have to consult on the colour photographs we are soon going to receive. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any other evidence in rejoinder the Defence intends to present?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we talked about this before, before these photographs, and we had thought not, but we don't know what we are going to discover now. So under this reservation, in all likelihood there would only be this evidence to be adduced in rejoinder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I, therefore, do understand that the picture that has been admitted into evidence, that is, the P3808, as such was not a reason to suggest any --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honour. Anyway, we had decided to bring this expert again for the following reason: The expert sent us by facsimile what he was able to, namely certain plans, layouts, but he was not able to locate particular wounds. So on the basis of this first photograph, he was unable to give us any information. He indicated that there were several possibilities. Today, however, things are a bit clearer, and therefore he should be given the opportunity of viewing this photograph again plus the other photographs and tell us what he thinks. We believe he should come here to tell us to what extent the first photograph can prove anything from the technical point of view. So in any case, we would like him to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So irrespective of what the other photographs will bring you, it is the request of the Defence to be permitted to present as rejoinder evidence the testimony of Dr. Dunjic, specifically in respect of Witness G and the new photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite so, Your Honour. Professor Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You certainly are aware that the Chamber did not permit any further expertise, apart from just the photographs. But we'll consider the matter and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is obvious that this witness should talk to us, if at all, only with regard to the evidence newly led by the Prosecution, namely these photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, is the Prosecution in a position to express itself immediately on the request to present Dr. Dunjic in respect of the photographs you -- that is admitted into evidence and the photographs still to be disclosed in coloured version to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd be grateful for the benefit of the morning break before I make some oral submissions in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I do anticipate I could do so straight after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There are a few things I'd like to check first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could do that. And then perhaps I could inform the parties as well as to the time schedule the Chamber has in mind. And of course there are two scenarios: The one is that the Defence will be allowed to present evidence in rejoinder; and the scenario where there would be no evidence in rejoinder. The -- if there will be any rejoinder evidence to be presented, the Chamber expects it to be done next week Tuesday or Wednesday. If rejoinder evidence will be presented, the parties are expected to submit their final briefs by the 23rd of April. This would give you three weeks for preparation, which is one week more than the Chamber initially had in mind. Closing argument is then expected to take place on the 6th and the 7th of May, one day for each party. If no evidence in rejoinder will be presented or be permitted to be presented, the final briefs should then be filed one week earlier; that would be the 16th of April. But the dates for the closing argument would not change; that would still be the 6th and the 7th of May. Also in that case the parties would have three weeks to prepare their final briefs and would then have three weeks to prepare for closing argument; whereas if the final briefs are submitted on the 23rd, there would be two weeks left to prepare for the closing arguments. This is what the Chamber has in mind. The Chamber after the break will hear from the parties what -- unless there's something that could not wait until 11.00, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Just one thing I want to say now: We saw that this witness could be recalled, and you haven't made provision for it in your schedule. Could you tell us after the break when, if necessary, he could be recalled. That's the only question in my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider whether it would be still in this week, which has been reserved for evidence -- rebuttal evidence, or that it would be wiser to do it just prior to the examination of Dr. Dunjic, if the Chamber would allow him to be called as evidence -- to give his testimony in rejoinder. We'll consider that. We'll adjourn until 11.00. The Chamber takes it that we'll need only a couple of minutes after 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is the issue of the admissibility of the tape 5 I think to be considered as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that we have -- let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I should say the compilation tape. There are some other little issues to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's just a matter of deciding, I think. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: More or less. But perhaps -- I'll raise it after 11.00. I simply rose to my feet because you said it was just a few minutes involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll deal with that matter after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a few matters still to be discussed. The first one is the position of the Prosecution in respect of the rejoinder evidence suggested by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution opposes the application by the Defence to call rejoinder evidence. There are two relevant considerations. The first is that the Defence expert did not seek access to Witness G for an inspection of him. That emerged from the cross-examination of the expert. Secondly, the Prosecution made an application to call a doctor who had examined Witness G a few weeks ago. That doctor was in a position to confirm where the wounds were and, secondly, comment on --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have to make an objection. I think that we took it that following your previous decisions we weren't to talk -- we weren't to discuss anything about this new element that appeared in Mr. Ierace's response, and I think we're looking for a shortcut again in order to address an issue that shouldn't be addressed. That's not exactly what I said, for the English booth. I said one wants to centre something -- place something in the centre of the debate, whereas you said that it should have been removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're talking about the expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly, Mr. President. I'm talking about these last scientific elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber allowed the Prosecution to present the witness who took the photographs, which could be understood as mainly to establish whether there might have been a mistake as to the right or to the left in a medical report. As I said before the break the Defence was aware of this limited scope of the rebuttal evidence accepted. The Defence now seeks to have further -- at least that's how I understand it -- further expertise on the basis of these photographs, in order to interpret them, to tell us in what respect this would change or confirm the earlier expertise. We therefore have to consider to what extent the previous ruling on excluding an expert report on specifically these woundings would have any consequence. I think that there was no need at this very moment to interrupt and Mr. Ierace could express himself as he deems fit. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. All I would add is that the decision of the Trial Chamber to exclude this further Prosecution evidence would, in my respectful submission, be a little inconsistent with any decision to permit the recalling of the Defence expert. That's all I wish to say on that matter, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. There is one matter that is interesting. Everyone can remember that the expert Mr. Dunjic, whom we have heard, said that one could distinguish an entry wound from an exit wound. I admit that I find it very difficult to identify -- to find the wounds on the back of this patient, and I think that the main question that we have to ask is to know whether the expert can identify on the basis of the photographs what would be an entry wound and what would be an exit wound on the basis of his experience, and that is strictly in relation to the photograph or photographs. And it's not in relation to the general technical problems. It has to do with the photograph and the testimony that was provided. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber takes it that there's no need for any further written submissions in this respect, and we'll take a decision in due course and inform the parties as soon as the decision has been reached, even if it would not be available yet in writing so that the parties can continue their preparation. Then, Mr. Ierace, you raised the issue of the three sequences out of the fifth videotape. Would you like to add something to what has been said in this respect until now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No further observations the Defence, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. But we quite clearly said there was a problem -- since there was some incomprehension last time, we clearly stated this, and we'll repeat it. The fairest solution would be to say - and I think that the Prosecution suggested this at the time - since we had this problem with the number 5 yesterday and today as well, except suppress -- delete the first sequence of our cassette which comes from tape number 5, rather than receiving three sequences from tape number 5, with regard to which neither the witness nor ourselves nor you can clearly carry out investigations. That should be the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace, if the Chamber would decide not to admit into evidence the three sequences, would you insist on non-admission of the first sequence of the compilation of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Indeed, as I've expressed in Mr. Piletta-Zanin's absence early last week reiterated on Friday, I don't seek that the Defence clips be removed from their exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's a separate issue of disclosure and the opportunity to present that material to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the matter, and the Chamber has to assume that the videotape deals with events that are outside the indictment period and therefore are of very limited relevance. In view of the evidence presented in respect of events similar like the ones that appear on the videotape and are within the indictment period, the Chamber considers the relevance of these three sequences not sufficient to admit them into evidence and keeps in mind that we would have to recall Mr. Gray for certain if we would admit them into evidence. Therefore, this evidence is -- this videotape and the transcript is not admitted into evidence. Then the Chamber invited the parties to comment on the suggested time schedule as I gave it to you just before the break. Mr. Ierace, is there any comment in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There's three things I'd like to say: Firstly, I note that the timetable allows, as I understand it, for one day for oral submissions by the Prosecution and one day for oral submissions by the Defence. Mr. President, I had intended to file a motion later today, indeed straight after today's proceedings, seeking an extension of space for the written submissions from the limit of 200 pages. So perhaps I could deal with that issue together and orally. Mr. President, this has been an extraordinarily complex trial, not only because of the number of witnesses that we have heard and not only because one aspect of the Prosecution case is circumstantial, but also, unusually, because of the temporal breadth of the evidence. We're talking about a period of almost two years. Mr. President, further, there are many technical aspects to the evidence. Additionally, there are a large number of exhibits which have been generated in the courtroom, maps and the like. Mr. President, it's my submission that the Prosecution, at least - I don't know about the Defence - could not do justice to the presentation of its case without a doubling of the number of pages, the maximum number of pages, and without two days to present oral argument. In support of the latter part of that submission, I note that in past trials two days has been permitted by the Prosecution and Defence each to make their submissions and by past trials - I have in mind trials of some length - to give two examples, in the trials of the Prosecutor and Blaskic and the Prosecutor and Krstic. Mr. President, I hasten to add that in oral submissions, and indeed in written submissions, the Prosecution has no intention of canvassing every little bit of evidence or laboriously summarising the evidence of Prosecution and Defence witnesses. We see this as an opportunity to bring together pieces of evidence which may not, in the manner in which they were presented in the sequence of the calling of witnesses under categories, have at first glance seemed to be linked. To give one simple example of that, there have been multiple witnesses who have given evidence in relation to activities in particular areas of Sarajevo and the confrontation lines. It's my respectful submission that the Trial Chamber may well be interested in bringing together of those different pieces of evidence in a way which gives added significance to them. Mr. President, I also hasten to add that I have no intention of drawing the attention of the Trial Chamber in either written form or oral form to every unscheduled sniping or shelling incident. In other words, we do intend to exercise judgment in the way in which we present the material and also in respect of the aspects of the evidence. Having said that, Mr. President, it's still, in my respectful submission, not possible to do justice in the scope of 200 written pages and four hours or thereabouts of oral submissions to this case. So Mr. President, I would be very grateful if -- if the Trial Chamber could give consideration -- and if I could say this: In proposing the 400 pages and the two days, I am not playing a game of making an ambit claim. I do think that we do need two days to -- which would be in the order of some eight hours to present our oral argument and 400 pages to do justice to our written submissions. Mr. President, I also add that we will do our best to develop a smooth presentation of the visual exhibits, if I could call it that. Mr. President, what I can offer, if it's of any assistance to the Trial Chamber and to the Defence, is that we would be prepared -- we would be in a position to present our oral submissions, our oral argument, whether or not there is rejoinder, a week earlier than the timetable presently provides. So if that's of any assistance, rather than presenting oral submissions on the 6th of May, we could do so one week earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I can respond to that immediately. As you may remember, I think we said before that the Chamber would have one week off and that unfortunately now coincides with the week previous to the suggested week. So therefore, we could not start on the 29th or the 30th of April because the Chamber is not available.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, that otherwise one would expect that if the -- if the final briefs would be filed one week earlier, that we would hear the oral argument also one week earlier, but the Chamber is just not there and has made all kind of arrangements which it cannot change any more, unfortunately. But that's the situation. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in French there is a proverb that says, "A good listener but someone who uses few words." No, no, for the English booth. I think that everyone has understood me. The Prosecution needed six minutes to develop two arguments. Could I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In less than six minutes: 200 pages we will stick to this. The Defence doesn't have the time to read 400 pages, to discuss them, to prepare for them, and Defence counsel is certain too that it will be able to make itself understood orally in one day of hearing. The conclusion is that both parties should one day be in a position to ensure that this proceeds better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Totally unclear to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
